Your municipal treasurer takes the first payment, and after January 31 the La Crosse County Treasurer handles it. The county office is in the Administration Center at 212 6th Street North, La Crosse, WI 54601. Call (608) 785-9711, write to treasurer@lacrossecounty.org, or stop by Monday to Friday, 8:00 am to 4:30 pm.

The dividing rule is Wis. Stat. 74.11(6). Money in by January 31 stays with the taxation district treasurer, and every other payment is the county's. For the amount of a first installment, ask the treasurer of your city, village or town. After the first deadline, call the county.

Assessments are a separate job. The county's Zoning and Land Information office keeps parcel records and the public property portal (608-785-9722), but the municipal assessor sets the values. County staff must carry the assessor's numbers and cannot change them, so a disagreement goes to the assessor first.

One option is the whole bill by January 31. The other is two installments, one due January 31 and one due July 31. Wis. Stat. 74.11(2) allows two installments, unless the real property tax on a parcel totals under $100, in which case it is due in full by January 31. A municipality can adopt a three-installment ordinance under 74.12, so ask your local treasurer if your bill has more than two payment slips.

Neither 2027 date is a business day. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, which stretches the five-working-day window to Friday, February 5, 2027 (74.11(7)(b)). July 31, 2027 is a Saturday, and its window runs to Friday, August 6, 2027 (74.11(8)(b)). Mailing early is still the safer choice. Section 74.69(1) treats a postmarked payment as timely when it reaches the right official within five business days of the due date.

A late bill is charged 1.5 percent monthly on what is unpaid, and the installment option disappears. The 1 percent is from Wis. Stat. 74.47(1), and La Crosse County Ordinance 4.05 adds the 0.5 percent penalty that 74.47(2) allows. Each is counted per month or fraction of a month, reaching back to February 1.

A few rules control what happens next:

  • Miss the first installment deadline and the full remaining balance is delinquent from February 1 (74.11(7)).
  • Delinquent real property tax, with interest and penalty, is paid to the county treasurer (74.11(11)).
  • A short payment is applied in a fixed order under 74.12(11)(a): personal property taxes first, then delinquent utility charges, special charges, special assessments and special taxes, with real property tax last.
  • Treasurers cannot waive interest for hardship. The only exceptions are a severe postal error and active military deployment of 90 days or more.

If you cannot cover an installment, pay what you can by the deadline and keep paying every month. Because of the application order, a partial payment may go to a special charge before it reaches the tax itself.

Four main jurisdictions appear on the bill: the county, the school district, the technical college and your municipality. A parcel inside a lake district or sanitary district carries that district's share too. The net assessed value rate is the combined mill rate of every jurisdiction, applied to your total assessed value, and the product is your tax before the lottery credit.

The estimated fair market value on the bill is calculated by the Department of Revenue from arm's-length sales in the past year. It is not an appraisal and not a prediction of your sale price. The average assessment ratio compares your municipality's assessed values with market value. Land and improvements are taxed at the same rate even when their values differ, and state law requires recently passed referenda to be listed.

No bill by December 21? Call your municipal treasurer. A missing bill does not stop interest from running (74.09(6)).

Your municipality's assessor is the first stop, and the municipal Board of Review is the second. In the City of La Crosse, the Assessor's Office is at 608-789-7525 (assessor@cityoflacrosse.org), and the City Clerk's Office at 608-789-7510 takes Board of Review filings. The city says an informal review answers most questions. If you still disagree, let the city clerk know, in writing or by voice, 48 hours or more before the board opens, then file an approved objection form before or within the first two hours of the first meeting.

The city calls its Board of Review a quasi-judicial body of five appointed residents that works like a court. It weighs the facts offered at the hearing, and the owner must show the property is assessed unfairly compared with the general level of assessment in the district. The calendar comes from state law, with sessions held in the 45 days starting the fourth Monday of April (70.47(1)).

A court can review the board's decision by certiorari, filed within 90 days after the decision notice (70.47(13)). Outside the city, ask the village or town clerk for the schedule.

Names on a tax bill come from recorded documents at the Register of Deeds, so ownership problems show up on the bill first. The county's Real Property FAQ gives several practical rules:

  • After a divorce, the former spouse's name stays on bills and notices until a recorded document, such as a quit claim deed or divorce judgment, changes title.
  • When an owner dies, a parcel held in joint tenancy or as survivorship marital property is cleared with a Termination of Decedent's Interest form filed at the Register of Deeds. Other kinds of title may call for an attorney and probate.
  • A parcel split during the year is billed as a whole to the owner at the time of the split, and the new parcels are assessed and taxed the next year. Assessments describe the property as of January 1.
  • Mailing address changes go through the municipal treasurer or the county office.
  • The public portal searches by owner name, address, parcel number or tax bill number, and the parcel format is ##-#####-### with zeros filled in.

If the contract is silent on taxes at delivery of the deed, Wis. Stat. 74.15 supplies the split. The seller owes the buyer one-twelfth of last year's tax for each month before the deed, and the sale month too when the deed lands after the 15th. For a payoff on delinquent tax, call the County Treasurer. Selling for cash leaves this untouched; the payoff is still taken from the proceeds at closing.

Three state programs can lower what an owner pays. The Lottery Credit is meant for Wisconsin homeowners who occupied the home as their primary residence on January 1, and you apply through the Department of Revenue. Completed applications reach the county monthly. If you claim after the first installment date, upload a copy or photo of your latest tax bill before October 1. Once granted, the credit remains until the owner or the department removes it.

The Homestead Credit is filed with state income taxes and helps lower-income owners. Disabled service members and surviving spouses can ask the County service office about a separate state property tax credit. Owners who struggle to pay can also talk with the County Treasurer about monthly payments, because smaller regular payments reduce the interest that builds up.

La Crosse County is the most populous county on Wisconsin's western border, with Minnesota across the river. The city of La Crosse is the seat. The county has two cities, La Crosse and Onalaska, and villages including Bangor, Holmen, Rockland and West Salem.

Population is 121,339 and there are 55,407 housing units. Owners occupy about 62.2 percent of homes. The median home value is $257,000, median gross rent is $1,059 and median household income is $73,013. Winters are cold, with January highs averaging 25.9 degrees, so heating costs and roof condition are fair topics for a buyer's inspection.

faqs.q: When are La Crosse County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Either the full amount by January 31 or two payments, January 31 and July 31. Your municipal treasurer receives payments through January 31, and the La Crosse County Treasurer receives later ones.

faqs.q: How much interest does La Crosse County charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: 1 percent monthly under Wis. Stat. 74.47, plus a 0.5 percent monthly penalty from county ordinance 4.05, all counted from February 1. A treasurer cannot waive it for hardship.

faqs.q: Where is the La Crosse County Treasurer's office?
faqs.a: Inside the Administration Center, 212 6th Street North, La Crosse, WI 54601. Call (608) 785-9711. It is staffed weekdays from 8:00 am until 4:30 pm.

faqs.q: Who can change my property assessment in La Crosse County?
faqs.a: Only your municipal assessor and, on appeal, the municipal Board of Review. The county's land information office maintains the values the assessor sets. In the City of La Crosse, call the Assessor's Office at 608-789-7525.

faqs.q: How do I remove a deceased spouse's name from a La Crosse County tax bill?
faqs.a: For a home owned in joint tenancy or as survivorship marital property, the Register of Deeds takes a Termination of Decedent's Interest form. For other ownership types an attorney may have to transfer title, possibly in probate.
